paragraphs.heading: Frozen seawater
paragraphs.text: Sea ice forms when seawater freezes. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats on the ocean's surface, just as fresh water ice does. It covers roughly 7% of Earth's whole surface and roughly 12% of the world's oceans. Much of it lies within the polar ice packs of Earth's polar regions. One is the Arctic ice pack, in the Arctic Ocean, and the other is the Antarctic ice pack, in the Southern Ocean. Icebergs are something different: they are chunks of glaciers or ice shelves that calve into the sea.

paragraphs.heading: Its part in the climate
paragraphs.text: Sea ice has a key part in Earth's climate. Its white surface sends the Sun's energy back to space. This is known as the albedo effect, and it helps to keep the planet cool. The ice also insulates the ocean beneath it, limiting how much heat, water vapor and gases such as carbon dioxide pass between the sea and the atmosphere. Whether sea ice is present or absent also shapes regional weather, global ocean circulation and the routes used for navigation.

paragraphs.heading: Seasons and the recent decline
paragraphs.text: The polar packs naturally go through a significant yearly cycle. Their surface extent is greatest in winter, and they retreat in summer. In recent decades, satellite records have also shown a marked decline in both the extent and the thickness of Arctic sea ice, and this trend is linked to global climate change. Antarctic sea ice shows more regional variability, but it too has recently been declining.

paragraphs.heading: Ice that keeps changing
paragraphs.text: Sea ice does not simply grow and melt. Over its lifespan it is very dynamic. Winds, currents and changes in water and air temperature act on it together, and as a result expanses of sea ice typically undergo a significant amount of deformation. This action leads to a wide variety of ice types and features.

paragraphs.heading: Fast ice and drift ice
paragraphs.text: One way to classify sea ice is by whether it is attached to the shoreline. Ice that is attached is known as landfast ice. More often it is just called fast ice, with fast meaning fastened. Drift ice is found further offshore, over very wide areas, and is free to move with currents and winds. It is made of floes: separate pieces of sea ice that measure at least 20 metres (66 ft) across. Floe sizes have names, from small, at 20 to 100 m, up to giant, at more than 10 km.

paragraphs.heading: What sea ice is made of
paragraphs.text: Sea ice is a composite material made of pure ice, liquid brine, air and salt. The shares of ice, brine and air by volume determine its key physical properties, including density and mechanical strength. While the ice is growing, brine typically makes up less than 5% of its bulk volume. The density of first-year ice changes strongly with the seasons. In winter it is higher, around 910–920 kg/m³, and in summer it is lower, around 860–880 kg/m³.

paragraphs.heading: Ages of ice, and life inside it
paragraphs.text: Scientists also classify sea ice by age, meaning its stage of development. The named stages are new ice, nilas, young ice, first-year ice and old ice. New ice is a general term for sea water that has frozen recently but is not yet solid ice. Sea ice also holds life: salty brine channels inside the ice are a habitat for microorganisms, and these form the base of unique food webs.
